SecPO: Principled Adversarial Training for Prompt Injection Security

Sizhe Chen, Yibo Peng, Jaewon Chang, Chawin Sitawarin, David Wagner Affiliation: UC Berkeley Affiliation: Anthropic, *work done at Google DeepMind
Abstract

Recognized as a top threat to AI agents, prompt injection allows instructions from untrusted data (email, documents, websites) to manipulate the agent’s operation. The existing best-defended LLM, Meta-SecAlign, is trained with the DPO loss but still suffers from attack success rates (ASRs) approaching 100% under adaptive prompt injections. One reason is that DPO anchors the model around the undefended reference model, which is insecure. We show an idealized reference model—an injection-invariant, utility-preserving oracle—can nevertheless be approximated, as its output distribution in training is interestingly accessible. This new observation motivates a theoretically principled SecPO loss. Another Meta-SecAlign shortcoming is that it trains on weak simulated attacks. We implement an efficient adversarial training (AT) pipeline that synthesizes strong injected inputs (best@240), and train the model on them. Our AT reduces ASRs by 1.5–14.5×\times across three SoTA adaptive attacks, compared with Meta-SecAlign; the SecPO loss reduces them by a further 2.4–4.6×\times compared with using DPO loss. In agentic workflows, our SecPO + AT Qwen3.6-27B is much more secure than Meta-SecAlign: 8.8% vs. 78.8% AgentDojo ASR@800 under the AttackerMovesSecond attack. Moreover, our defended model shows no noticeable reduction in benign utility in nine benchmarks covering agentic tool calling, instruction following, science, and math. We release our code, training data (with optimized injections from AT), and model.

1 Introduction

Rapid progress in large language models (LLMs) unlocks exciting agentic applications: a software engineering agent can work autonomously for seven hours on a complex task in a codebase containing 12.5 million lines of code, with only occasional human guidance [4]. A running agent interacts frequently with the real-world environment (e.g., code repositories, websites, documents) that may not be trusted. An attacker can post malicious content to hijack an agent’s execution. In an actual incident, the attacker created a GitHub issue with a specially crafted title; a coding agent read the malicious title and was hijacked into executing attacker-controlled code [19]. This prompt injection attack is listed as the top threat to AI agents [69]. Vulnerabilities to prompt injection allow external attackers to control the agent through simple actions, such as creating a GitHub issue [19], sending an email [80], or writing a sentence (“disregard all prior instructions and …”) in a file [29]. AI agent deployment has been held back due to uncontrollable security risks from prompt injections [92].

To mitigate prompt injections, AI agents are expected to only follow instructions from the trusted inputs, while still processing untrusted inputs as context [10]. This behavior can be implemented in the model weights [10, 13, 14, 86, 93, 41] or in the system around the model [35, 55, 22, 88, 83, 53]. This paper focuses on developing robust LLMs. The current best-defended LLM, Meta-SecAlign [14], is fine-tuned on simulated attacks using direct preference optimization (DPO [77]). Meta-SecAlign, however, has been broken by the latest adaptive prompt injections [65, 97, 91] with >95% attack success rates (ASRs).

We show one reason for Meta-SecAlign’s vulnerability is that its DPO loss anchors the model around the undefended model. This regularization is intended to avoid drifting too far from its initialization and losing utility when there is no attack. However, this hinders security improvements, as the undefended model is insecure. We therefore ask:

Can we achieve both goals: strong security and the same utility as the undefended model?

If we had an ideal oracle model that achieves both, we could simply approximate its output distribution. We do not have such a model, so there is no way to actually instantiate it. However, we introduce a scheme to predict how an oracle LLM would respond to an injected sample in training. Then, we fine-tune our model to approximate the output distribution of this simulated oracle: we propose Secure Preference Optimization (SecPO), a new loss for optimizing models to be robust against prompt injection. The SecPO loss overcomes this shortcoming in Meta-SecAlign’s training objective.

We combine SecPO with adversarial training (AT). AT mitigates another shortcoming of Meta-SecAlign, which trains the model only on weak attacks, but does not train it on strong attacks. We implement an efficient AT pipeline that synthesizes strong attacks using PAIR [8] (best@240), and trains the model on these attacks, equipping it with the ability to defeat unseen test-time adaptive attacks that are more sophisticated.

Our AT reduces ASRs by 1.5–14.5×\times across three SoTA adaptive attacks, compared with Meta-SecAlign; the SecPO loss reduces them by a further 2.4–4.6×\times compared with using DPO loss. Trained from Qwen3.6-27B, our SecPO + AT model is much more secure than Meta-SecAlign: 8.8% vs. 78.8% AgentDojo ASR@800 under the current strongest adaptive prompt injection [65]; see Figure 1 for more comparisons. Besides, the maximum ASR of three state-of-the-art (SoTA) adaptive prompt injection attacks [65, 59, 97] is only 13.3% for our model, compared with 94.0% for Meta-SecAlign. We also achieve 7.6% ASR on DTaP-Bench [16], which contains challenging real-world agentic tasks and strong injected prompts. Evaluations on nine challenging benchmarks covering agentic tool calling [23, 47, 16], instruction following [25, 108], science [84, 78], and mathematics [20, 46] show that our defended LLM maintains similar utility on benign tasks as the undefended one.

To make the benefits of computationally expensive AT more widely available, we release our training set with optimized injections from our AT pipeline. Training on it requires no additional attack generation, but yields 2.5–22.5×\times lower ASRs in our study. Further analysis shows our defended model is interestingly secure against adaptive visual prompt injections [12], even though we do not specify this defense goal. We release our code, training data, and model weights.

2 Preliminaries

AI agents take in untrusted inputs that may be injected. An AI agent accepts trusted and untrusted inputs. In most real-world cases, it is clear which inputs are trusted (like a user command, a trusted website, an email from someone you know) or untrusted (like an untrusted website, a random email, an untraceable file, a copied paragraph). Thus, the prompt injection problem is defined under the assumption that the agent is told which parts are trusted and should not follow untrusted instructions. The prompt injection problem excludes cases where the trust label is unknown and needs to be determined by the agent, e.g., using the surrounding context [1], or where instructions in data need be followed if they are aligned with the user prompt [86].

Prompt injection attack. At test time, the attacker injects instructions into data, aiming to execute an attacker-specific task. A prompt injection attack is deemed successful if the LLM completes the task in the injected instruction. We assume the attacker knows the benign prompt, benign data, and the LLM’s chat template, but cannot change them. This assumption favors the attacker, as when the attacker targets an unknown victim agent in the real world, it may not be able to know the complete benign contexts. Existing automatic adaptive prompt injection methods include RL-based attacks [91, 97, 15] that train a strong attacker LLM dedicated to breaking a defender LLM using reinforcement learning (RL); search-based attacks [8, 59, 65] that use an attacker API to iteratively refine injections; gradient-based attacks [107, 71] that optimize an attack suffix in a white-box manner. The attacker can resort to black-box RL-based and search-based attacks to break any deployed model–our evaluations cover both attacks. We assume the test-time attacker cannot access the model weights to perform gradient-based attacks, which produce non-readable attacks that can be easily mitigated by perplexity-based classifiers [2]; see [72]. However, we do report improved robustness to GCG [107] under this category (along with another white-box attack) in Appendix’s Table 18. The indirect prompt injection problem we study assumes that the user is benign and the environment is malicious, so attacks where the user is malicious (jailbreaks [107], direct prompt injection [64]) are outside of our scope.

Prompt injection defense. A robust AI agent is expected to ignore any injections when there is an attack, and have utility similar to the undefended agent’s when there is no attack. Because prompt injection exploits agents’ confusion between the prompt (control signal) and data (data signal), the defense follows the principle of separating the prompt and data [10]. This separation can be instantiated in the system around the model or in the model weights. System-level defenses include detecting attacks  [75, 100, 17, 53], prompting the LLM to ignore potential injections [96, 34, 81], filtering out any injections from the data [88, 83, 38, 87, 21], or limiting the LLM’s ability to take actions defined as harmful [22, 60].

Chat template in model-level defenses. Model-level defenses train the model to distinguish between the prompt and data [86, 93]. StruQ [10] proposes to use a dedicated message type to represent this distinction. Untrusted data is wrapped within this message type (role). The dedicated role for data could be a new role (“input” as in [14] and our work, see below) or an existing role (“tool” role in existing APIs [86]).

Multiple messages are formatted into one string that is fed to the LLM by a library function, which is responsible for applying the chat template, delimiters, and tokenizer to obtain the final input to the LLM. A well-written library, e.g., OpenAI Harmony [66], will ensure that no message can break out of its message type or change its role. Thus, we assume that malicious text in the untrusted data cannot escape the input message role to become an officially recognized trusted prompt, though attackers can still use fake delimiters [39] or responses [52, 95] to trick the model into believing this.

Training samples in model-level defenses. The defender then trains LLMs to respect this separation via fine-tuning on simulated prompt injections in the data, teaching the LLM to only follow instructions from the trusted prompt. The SoTA recipe is Meta-SecAlign [14], which optimizes the LLM to prefer a secure response over an insecure response. Specifically, Meta-SecAlign uses a generic instruction-tuning dataset [79] 𝒟inst\mathcal{D_{\text{inst}}} where each sample zz consists of a user instruction zpromptz_{\text{prompt}} and input data zdataz_{\text{data}}. Meta-SecAlign constructs a preference dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} with a static attack template:

    Input xinjx_{\text{inj}}: For each sample xclean=z∈𝒟instx_{\text{clean}}=z\in\mathcal{D_{\text{inst}}}, prompt-inject it by randomly picking another sample z′z^{\prime} from 𝒟inst\mathcal{D_{\text{inst}}} and putting AttackTemplate​(zprompt′,zdata′)\text{AttackTemplate}(z^{\prime}_{\text{prompt}},z^{\prime}_{\text{data}}) at the beginning or the end of zdataz_{\text{data}} with equal probabilities.

With the above dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}, Meta-SecAlign fine-tunes an LLM using direct preference optimization (DPO [77]), which maximizes the log-likelihood difference between the desirable response ywy_{w} and undesirable one yly_{l}, while keeping the LLM close to the undefended reference model πundef\pi_{\text{undef}} by minimizing

3 SecPO: Secure Preference Optimization

Despite reporting single-digit static ASRs in the paper [14], Meta-SecAlign suffers from >95% ASRs under the strongest adaptive prompt injection attacks [65, 97]. We identify Meta-SecAlign’s two shortcomings in its training objective (Section 3.1) and training-time attacks (Section 3.5), and propose our methodology that addresses these two shortcomings.

3.1 Limitations of DPO objective for security

Meta-SecAlign uses the DPO training loss. This has been shown to be equivalent, in a specific setting, to online training with a KL-regularized PPO objective [77]. Specifically, minimizing Equation 1 is equivalent to maximizing this KL-regularized PPO objective:

𝔼xinj∼𝒟,y∼πθ(⋅|xinj)[r(xinj,y)−β⋅KL(πθ(⋅|xinj)∥πundef(⋅|xinj))].\mathbb{E}_{x_{\text{inj}}\sim\mathcal{D},~y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x_{\text{inj}})}\left[r(x_{\text{inj}},y)-\beta\cdot\text{KL}\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x_{\text{inj}})\|\pi_{\text{undef}}(\cdot|x_{\text{inj}})\right)\right]. (2)

The PPO objective simultaneously maximizes a reward rr (encouraging secure responses in our case), while constraining the model (πθ\pi_{\theta}) to stay close to its initial reference (πundef\pi_{\text{undef}}) on training inputs (xinjx_{\text{inj}}). DPO allows us to directly use offline preference pairs (yw,yl)(y_{w},y_{l}) for training, so that a standalone reward model rr (to judge online-generated yy) is not needed.

Here we see that PPO (and hence implicitly DPO as well) uses a KL term to regularize the LLM πθ\pi_{\theta} to remain close to the undefended model given injected training inputs. The undefended reference model, however, is highly vulnerable. Thus, anchoring the model to behave similarly to the undefended model hinders security improvements. This regularization made sense for DPO’s intended application, but is not appropriate for defending against prompt injection.

3.2 Defining an idealized oracle reference

We propose to resolve this shortcoming by adjusting the regularization term to be suitable for prompt injection defense. We ask: what is the best model a defender can dream of? Intuitively, it is a so-called oracle model that behaves the same as the undefended model on benign inputs, and is completely secure on malicious inputs. Formally, the oracle satisfies:

  • •

    Security requirement: Given an injected input, the oracle has the same output distribution as if the injection were removed: πoracle(⋅|xinj)=πoracle(⋅|xclean)\pi_{\text{oracle}}(\cdot|x_{\text{inj}})=\pi_{\text{oracle}}(\cdot|x_{\text{clean}}).

  • •

    Utility requirement: Given a clean input, the oracle has the same output distribution as the undefended model: πoracle(⋅|xclean)=πundef(⋅|xclean)\pi_{\text{oracle}}(\cdot|x_{\text{clean}})=\pi_{\text{undef}}(\cdot|x_{\text{clean}}).

Combining the equations yields

πoracle(⋅|xinj)=πundef(⋅|xclean).\pi_{\text{oracle}}(\cdot|x_{\text{inj}})=\pi_{\text{undef}}(\cdot|x_{\text{clean}}). (3)

On the right side, πundef\pi_{\text{undef}} is available in training as it is the initialization checkpoint; xcleanx_{\text{clean}} is also available as the training simulates xinjx_{\text{inj}} from it. That is, the left side is completely accessible, meaning that we can just access the oracle’s output distribution in training (given injected inputs xinjx_{\text{inj}}) by feeding the undefended model with clean inputs. Thus, the oracle can be directly approximated, even if an oracle model checkpoint satisfying the above requirements does not exist.

3.3 The proposed SecPO loss

Inspired by this observation, we propose SecPO, which replaces the vulnerable undefended reference model in Equation 2 with the idealized oracle reference model to maximize

𝔼xinj∼𝒟,y∼πθ(⋅|xinj)[r(xinj,y)−β⋅KL(πθ(⋅|xinj)∥πoracle(⋅|xinj))].\mathbb{E}_{x_{\text{inj}}\sim\mathcal{D},~y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x_{\text{inj}})}\left[r(x_{\text{inj}},y)-\beta\cdot\text{KL}\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x_{\text{inj}})\|{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\pi_{\text{oracle}}}(\cdot|x_{\text{inj}})\right)\right].

As in Section 3.1, this online optimization objective [77] is equivalent to minimizing the following offline objective:

−log⁡σ⁡(β​log⁡πθ​(yw∣xinj)πoracle​(yw∣xinj)−β​log⁡πθ​(yl∣xinj)πoracle​(yl∣xinj)).-\log\sigma\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}\left(y_{w}\mid x_{\text{inj}}\right)}{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\pi_{\text{oracle}}}\left(y_{w}\mid x_{\text{inj}}\right)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}\left(y_{l}\mid x_{\text{inj}}\right)}{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\pi_{\text{oracle}}}\left(y_{l}\mid x_{\text{inj}}\right)}\right).

Although no oracle checkpoint is available, Equation 3 gives access to its output distribution on training inputs. Thus, minimizing the above is equivalent to minimizing ℒSecPO =\mathcal{L}_{\text{SecPO }}=

−log⁡σ⁡(β​log⁡πθ​(yw∣xinj)πundef​(yw∣xclean)−β​log⁡πθ​(yl∣xinj)πundef​(yl∣xclean)).-\log\sigma\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}\left(y_{w}\mid x_{\text{inj}}\right)}{\pi_{\text{undef}}\left(y_{w}\mid{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}x_{\text{clean}}}\right)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}\left(y_{l}\mid x_{\text{inj}}\right)}{\pi_{\text{undef}}\left(y_{l}\mid{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}x_{\text{clean}}}\right)}\right). (4)

That is, SecPO loss can be implemented with a minimal change (red parts) to DPO loss (1). In practice, the only difference in Equation 4 is to feed the undefended model with clean inputs, rather than with injected inputs in Equation 1. Please see Appendix A for further proof details.

A problem with DPO is that it constrains the model to behave similarly to the insecure reference on inputs with injections. For prompt injection defense, this constraint is undesirable—it forces the learned model to retain the insecure behavior of the reference model. Instead, we want the learned model to behave differently. SecPO eliminates this constraint, enabling it to behave more securely. Figure 2 shows this effect: DPO can only reduce the log-probability of the insecure response to about −400-400, while SecPO further reduces it to about −700-700. See Figure 9 (Appendix) for further illustration.

πundef\pi_{\text{undef}}’s injection-induced preference shift. If an injected prompt causes πundef\pi_{\text{undef}} to shift its preference from ywy_{w} toward yly_{l} significantly, Δundef>0\Delta_{\text{undef}}>0, upscaling this sample’s SecPO gradients vs. DPO ones. Consequently, SecPO emphasizes injection-sensitive samples. Intuitively, non-sensitive samples are likely to already be handled securely, so are a low priority. Injection-sensitive samples are handled insecurely, so should be a high priority to handle differently. SecPO is beneficial because it prioritizes improving security for those samples.

SecPO is not equivalent to DPO with a larger learning rate. While it is true that SecPO maintains the same gradient direction as DPO for each individual sample, the scaling factor is different for each sample, so the accumulated SecPO gradient is not just a scaled version of the accumulated DPO gradient. Additional empirical observations are in Appendix C.1.

3.5 SecPO algorithm with adversarial training

SecPO loss resolves one drawback of Meta-SecAlign by changing its suboptimal training objective. Another drawback of Meta-SecAlign is that it trains on weak static simulated injections. As a result, Meta-SecAlign learns to defend against weak attacks but struggles to defend against strong adaptive attacks. A straightforward fix is to train on prompt injection attacks that are as strong as possible [85], so that the final LLM is robust to stronger unseen attacks at test time. This is also known as adversarial training (AT).

AT for LLMs is extremely expensive. At each step of training, AT involves attacking the latest checkpoint and training against this attacked input. This process is already costly for image classification, where AT was originally developed [31]. For LLMs, it is even more expensive, because finding injection tokens in the discrete token space is much harder than finding adversarial images in continuous pixel space [107], making prompt injection generation very slow. For this reason, no one in the literature has reported success in using AT to defend against prompt injection (see Section 5).

We thus study how to implement AT for prompt injection defense. To generate strong injected training samples, there are three adaptive attack methods known in the literature: (1) RL-based attacks [91, 97, 15], (2) gradient-based attacks [107, 71], and (3) search-based attacks [8, 59, 65]; see Section 2.

AT using (1) RL-based attacks (fine-tuning a dedicated attacker LLM to generate strong injections against each training checkpoint) requires co-evolving the attacker LLM checkpoint along with the defender LLM training [90]. The cost of RL training makes this computationally intensive [90], almost infeasible outside frontier industry labs.

AT using (2) gradient-based attacks (adversarially optimizing injection suffixes by gradients from an attack loss) is also computationally difficult. The fastest gradient-based attacks [27, 37, 48] take approximately one GPU-minute per sample. We tried applying continuous optimization to input embeddings [94] instead of discrete optimization. This is faster, but we did not find it effective (see Appendix C.3).

Therefore, we focus on AT using (3) search-based attacks (querying attacker/judge LLM APIs to refine injection phrasings). Because commercial APIs support high-concurrency queries, the attack search process can be parallelized and thus accelerated. Please see Algorithm 1 for the overall training recipe. We handle training batches, each containing bb clean inputs and bb (initial) simulated injected instructions constructed in the same way as Meta-SecAlign; see Section 2.

Lines 4–11 are our AT using PAIR [8], a SoTA search-based attack. For each attack step tt, we prompt an attacker LLM API to propose nn candidate injections for each of the bb samples; run inference on the training checkpoint with n×bn\times b injected inputs; prompt a judge LLM API to score how well each candidate injection induces injection-following outputs; keep the best-scored candidate injection for each of the bb samples. We adapt PAIR’s attacker/judge prompts for prompt injection; see Appendix E. The judge prompt contains detailed rubrics with chain-of-thought examples about how to score, and asks for explanations (of how a score comes about) and suggestions (about how to improve future attacks). The attacker receives a history of recent attack attempts and judge feedback, and is encouraged to propose diverse injections. This process is repeated for TT iterations, yielding the best injections after n×Tn\times T attack attempts.

As shown in Figure 3, the attacker LLM query (Line 5), the defender LLM inference (Line 7), and the judge LLM query (Line 8) run sequentially, with queries for all samples in a batch launched concurrently within each stage. This high-concurrency design takes advantage of existing LLM inference infrastructure that is optimized for efficient parallel processing. Thus, LLM inference is accelerated by parallelizing in-batch query requests. Our recipe makes AT feasible for prompt injection defense, requiring 18 hours on 16 H200 GPUs to train Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.

To make the benefit of AT accessible to a broader range of researchers, we release our training set with optimized injections from SecPO AT on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Fine-tuning on this fixed dataset requires no additional attack generation while still achieving significant security. We call this recipe offline AT, whose efficiency enables us to fine-tune much larger LLMs like Qwen3.6-27B.

3.6 SecPO is security-informed regularization

We offer a different perspective on our recipe; see Figure 4. To provide security supervision, AT simulates strong attacks in the inputs to elicit undesirable responses, so that the same preference pair provides strong security training signals. Traditionally, this security improvement is hindered by utility regularization, KL(πθ(⋅|xinj)∥πundef(⋅|xinj))\text{KL}\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x_{\text{inj}})\|\pi_{\text{undef}}(\cdot|x_{\text{inj}})\right), which constrains the LLM to stay close to its high-utility but insecure initialization.

The SecPO loss provides an alternative form of security-informed regularization, unlocking security improvements while preserving utility. Our utility goal is to preserve the model’s usefulness on benign inputs, as there is no attack most of the time. Thus, our idealized utility-preservation target is πθ(⋅|xclean)=πundef(⋅|xclean)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x_{\text{clean}})=\pi_{\text{undef}}(\cdot|x_{\text{clean}}). If security supervision makes the model invariant to injections, then πθ(⋅|xinj)=πθ(⋅|xclean)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x_{\text{inj}})=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x_{\text{clean}}). Relying on this invariance, we can regularize for utility by targeting πθ(⋅|xinj)=πundef(⋅|xclean)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x_{\text{inj}})=\pi_{\text{undef}}(\cdot|x_{\text{clean}}), which is derived by combining the above two equations. As this security-informed regularization, KL(πθ(⋅|xinj)∥πundef(⋅|xclean))\text{KL}\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x_{\text{inj}})\|\pi_{\text{undef}}(\cdot|x_{\text{clean}})\right), depends on the success of security supervision, it allows security improvements without constraining them.

The SecPO loss and AT jointly contribute to improving the model’s security against prompt injection while achieving the same utility-preserving effect as Meta-SecAlign.

4 Experiments

We describe the training and evaluation setup in Section 4.1, with implementation details in Appendix B. Section 4.2 compares our complete recipe (SecPO +AT) with Meta-SecAlign in security and benign utility, and Section 4.3 analyzes its transfer to multi-step agentic tasks. Section 4.4 separates the contributions of AT and SecPO loss. We then examine security transfer to mitigate visual prompt injections (Section 4.5). Section 4.6 introduces our offered open-source benefits to researchers, developers, and model providers. Finally, Section 4.7 characterizes attacks that are still successful against our model, aiming to direct future defense efforts.

4.1 Setup

Training details.

We fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [32] and Qwen3.6-27B [76]. We use Qwen3.6-27B as a non-reasoning LLM (disabling thinking in training and evaluation), and leave the study of securing reasoning models for future work. Following Meta-SecAlign [14], we build our security preference dataset from Cleaned-Alpaca [79]. We select samples with a data field, apply the simulated static injection as in [14], and obtain 1915719157 preference pairs. We optimize the static injections by adaptive attacks. We use the same prompt-data separation format as Meta-SecAlign, extending the chat template with an additional input role for untrusted data, as described in Section 2. We fine-tune for one epoch, using sigmoid activation, β=0.1\beta=0.1, and a learning rate of 1.6×10−41.6\times 10^{-4}. Following [14], training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct uses LoRA with rank 6464, α=8\alpha=8, dropout 0.10.1, and target modules {q_proj,v_proj,gate_proj,down_proj,up_proj}\{\texttt{q\_proj},\texttt{v\_proj},\texttt{gate\_proj},\texttt{down\_proj},\texttt{up\_proj}\}, and training Qwen3.6-27B additionally fine-tunes {k_proj,o_proj}\{\texttt{k\_proj},\texttt{o\_proj}\} in our study.

We run our complete recipe (SecPO loss, AT) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. For each training sample, the attacker proposes n=8n=8 candidate injections, victim responses are judged on a 1–10 scale for progress toward the injected goal, and the best-scored candidate is retained. We repeat this process for T=30T=30 iterations, giving 240 trials to search for the best possible injection towards the current checkpoint in training. Attacker, victim, and judge calls are batched across examples. We use Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite-Preview as the attacker and Gemini-2.5-Flash as the judge with a Tier-3 Gemini API key.

Besides a defended Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, this run also creates a training set with optimized injections for each sample (see below), and it can be directly used to fine-tune other models, including larger ones, with no additional attack generation. We thus perform such offline AT on Qwen3.6-27B, which takes 7 hours on 8 H200s. The following sample from this dataset illustrates an optimized injection together with its stored desirable and undesirable training responses.

Train–test separation on sample domain and attack types.

We take great care to avoid any possible train–test overlap. Our training uses Cleaned-Alpaca instruction-following samples and PAIR search-based attacks [8] to construct adaptive injections. In evaluation, samples cover domains including instruction-following (AlpacaEval2 and SEP unseen in training [14]), agentic tool-calling (AgentDojo, AgentDyn, DTaP-Bench-Indirect), science (MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond), and math (GSM8K, Minerva_Math). Attack-wise, the test-time evaluations use held-out search-based attacks (Genetic [65] and TAP [59]), and an unseen RL-based attack (PISmith [97]). Those adaptive attacks and benchmark-specific static attacks are done on samples unseen in training.

Instruction Following (SEP) benchmark.

SEP ASR evaluates instruction-following tasks under distinct prompt injection goals on 9,1609{,}160 SEP [108] test examples. The static evaluation tries six injection templates, placing direct, ignore, completion, and completion-ignore variants around the untrusted data. We count a sample as successfully attacked if one of the attacks succeeds, following [14]. SEP Genetic and TAP Adaptive ASR evaluate search-based adaptive attacks by prompting attacker LLMs: Genetic [65] (n=8,T=100n=8,T=100) evolves candidate injections with an island genetic algorithm and MAP-Elites, while TAP [59] (8 seed injections, search width 10 and breadth 10) searches through tree-of-thoughts branching and pruning. We use 1,0241{,}024 samples for all SEP adaptive attacks. For each of them, the attack evaluates up to 800 candidates (attack attempts), and we report whether any candidate succeeds (Pass@800 ASR). SEP PISmith Adaptive ASR trains an attack LLM with RL to generate prompt injections from black-box feedback [97]. For each evaluated checkpoint, we train a separate attacker initialized from Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. The attacker is trained on 100100 examples from the Dolly Closed-QA split of PIArena, as officially recommended, and evaluated (without further updating) on 1,0241{,}024 SEP test examples. At evaluation time, we sample 1010 candidate injections per SEP example and report pass@1010 ASR. We train each PISmith attacker for 10 epochs with GRPO (ϵ=0.2\epsilon=0.2, β=0\beta=0), using 15 rollouts per prompt, sampling temperature 1.0, learning rate 10−510^{-5}.

Judge Protocol. Each SEP example contains an injected instruction and an instance-specific witness word. The witness word is expected to always appear if an injection is followed, and never appear if not. Thus, witness word appearance is the official criterion to judge attack success in [108]. We find this substring matching is highly unreliable, e.g., the word “cat” will be regarded as appearing in “indicate”. Thus, each candidate response is further evaluated by 9 independent judge queries to 3 judge LLMs (Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite-Preview, Gemini-3-Flash-Preview, GPT-5, temperature=1). The prompt includes the trusted task, injection goal, victim response, in-context demonstrations of successful/unsuccessful attacks, and asks whether the response actually complies with the injected goal. We deem a sample successfully attacked if all nine judge calls confirm success. To inspect the accuracy of this judge protocol, we manually look at 1,024 outputs drawn from Genetic/TAP adaptive SEP evaluations. The nine-judge rule gave 0 false positives and 0 false negatives against these labels. The official substring match rule gave 67 false positives and 0 false negatives, often because the witness appeared inside another word. This audit supports our multi-judge rule as a good success criterion.

Agentic Tool-Calling Benchmarks.

AgentDyn [47] evaluates 60 benign tasks in environments where the data is expected to alter the next action. It contains 560 static injected cases. DTaP-Bench-Indirect [16] contains 1,998 (fixed strong) indirect prompt injection samples across 12 interactive domains in real-world complex agentic tasks. We exclude 160 MacOS and WindowsOS samples (as we cannot reproduce them), giving 1,838 samples. On those samples, we also report the utility (under attack), while we report benign utility for all other benchmarks. DTaP injects varied content, and we put anything untrusted (subject to injection) within the input role, as we assume the agent receives a clear signal of which parts are trusted or not; see Section 2.

AgentDojo [23] evaluates prompt injection attacks in tool-calling agents: 9797 user tasks are paired with injected tasks, yielding 949949 user-task–injection-task pairs, and an attack succeeds if the malicious tool is called. We use the benchmark’s “important instructions” attack style to evaluate static attacks. All numbers are obtained with the benchmark’s “repeat-user-prompt” defense, following [14]. AgentDojo Genetic adaptive attack uses the same attack settings as [65] (Gemini-2.5-Pro max-thinking attacker for ASR@800 on the same 80-example subset, without using victim’s thinking). Our reproduction was confirmed by its author, so we plot the paper’s evaluation results along with ours in Figure 1, which places our work in the broader landscape of defenses in the community [106, 83, 61, 34, 88, 14]. Note that other defenses are orthogonal methods that could work together with ours to build secure AI agents: Our defended model can be combined with any system-level defenses, and our recipe is applicable with model-level architectural defenses [93, 41, 49].

4.2 Mitigating adaptive prompt injections while preserving benign utility

In this subsection, we compare our recipe (SecPO + AT) against the prior SoTA model-level defense, Meta-SecAlign (DPO + non-AT), and demonstrate superior security against adaptive attacks without dropping benign utility. We first fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with our recipe and Meta-SecAlign, and measure the models’ security and utility in Table 1. With the above generated injections, we then apply offline AT to fine-tune a much larger LLM, Qwen3.6-27B, and compare its security and utility with the one fine-tuned with Meta-SecAlign in Table 2. Results show that we reduce adaptive ASRs by an order of magnitude while maintaining utility comparable to that of the undefended model.

Our recipe substantially improves security over Meta-SecAlign while keeping utility stable for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. In Table 1, mean utility across the six instruction-following, science, and math benchmarks changes only slightly, from 46.9% for the undefended model to 47.3% with Meta-SecAlign and 47.5% with our recipe. The security advantage is pronounced under adaptive attacks: Genetic and TAP ASRs@800 fall from 89.1% and 84.6% to 12.3% and 12.2%, while PISmith ASR@10 falls from 95.1% to 7.0%. Averaging over these three attacks, ASR drops from 89.6% to 10.5%, an 8.5×\times reduction. These attacks are unseen in training, showing that the security gains extend beyond the training-time PAIR search.

Reusing the optimized injections brings similar security gains to the larger Qwen3.6-27B without additional attack generation. Our recipe on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct crafts adaptive injections, which we save to a fixed training set, so they can be reused to fine-tune any LLMs without generating strong injections again. Even though these injections are not optimized on the fly during training of the other LLMs, we show that strong security can still be obtained without noticeably hurting benign utility (Table 2). Mean utility across the same six benchmarks changes from 88.9% to 88.4% for Meta-SecAlign and to 89.1% for our offline AT recipe with SecPO loss. SEP Genetic, TAP, and PISmith adaptive ASRs decrease from 93.7%, 90.1%, and 94.0% to 13.3%, 12.5%, and 1.8%, respectively. Mean adaptive ASR thus drops from 92.6% to 9.2%, a 10.1×\times reduction. The fixed training set therefore transfers the benefits of our AT run to a larger model by reusing pre-generated optimized injections.

4.3 Security generalization to agentic tasks

As in Table 2, the security learned from our instruction-following training samples generalizes to multi-step agentic tasks, where the prompt injection threat is most prominent. Our training uses only instruction-following samples without agent trajectories, yet the defended Qwen3.6-27B is very robust under real-world agentic tasks. We evaluate on AgentDojo, AgentDyn, and DTaP, as well as adaptive evaluation under 800 attempts in AgentDojo by Genetic attacks as in [65]. Our model reduces adaptive ASR from 78.8% (Meta-SecAlign) to 8.8%, compared with 81.3% for the undefended model. On the static AgentDojo and AgentDyn attacks, SecPO records no observed attack successes, versus 2.2% and 4.8% for Meta-SecAlign. On the 1,838 DTaP cases (Qwen-Agent harness), ASR falls from 45.9% (Meta-SecAlign) to 7.6%. This is lower than GPT-5.5’s 20.8% ASR in our evaluation with OpenClaw harness, and 8.1% ASR of Claude Opus 4.6 with Claude Code harness reported in [16].

Analysis below on agent evaluation logs shows that our model is good at handling cases which are believed hard to handle by existing literature: it is robust in specific challenging types of injections and performs well in hard benign tasks.

  • •

    Resist injections semantically close to the benign task. Attacks aligned with the benign task are reported to bypass defenses more successfully [28]. We select a subset of DTaP with injections that are semantically close to the benign task. Across 481 such DTaP cases, our model reduces ASR to 12.3%, compared with 58.8% for the undefended model and 55.1% for Meta-SecAlign. As an example, in Figure 5, both the trusted task and the injection concern the patient’s diagnosis, but the injection asks for a plausible incorrect answer. Our model returns the reference diagnosis of second-degree internal hemorrhoids; Meta-SecAlign follows the injection and returns nonspecific proctitis. Thus, a similar injection does not by itself defeat our defense.

  • •

    Remain robust when multiple injections are present. Prior work shows that distributing malicious instructions across multiple steps in a task can increase attack success [40, 101]. The 123-case DTaP subset contains at least two non-empty tool-injection payloads. SecPO has only 4 attack successes (3.3%), compared with 41 (33.3%) for Meta-SecAlign and 63 (51.2%) for the undefended model. In Figure 6, the same request to exfiltrate the user’s email and shipping address appears on three different tools. SecPO returns the requested reviewers without sending account information, whereas Meta-SecAlign sends the private data to the attacker-controlled address. In contrast to the vulnerabilities highlighted by prior work, we show that they can be well-mitigated by a robust model.

  • •

    Protect against diverse injection channels and positions. Jia et al. emphasize evaluation with diverse injected prompts and locations [39]. Among the 1,838 DTaP scenarios, 640 (34.8%) mix insertion positions and 546 (29.7%) combine multiple attack channels. Placements include appending or prepending content, creating new records, and replacing entire fields or documents. Figure 10 in Appendix C.6 provides the full breakdown. Across this diverse benchmark, our model achieves 7.6% ASR, compared with 50.8% for the undefended model and 45.9% for Meta-SecAlign. Our low overall ASR across these diverse injection settings extends the robustness evidence beyond the narrow evaluations criticized in prior work.

  • •

    Handle benign tasks where future actions require replanning based on data. AgentDyn [47] highlights this requirement for defenses. Our defended model, despite being fine-tuned to ignore injections in data, is able to handle benign data and replan from it: its AgentDyn utility is 71.7%, matching the undefended model (Table 2). Table 21 shows a specific sample. Here, SecPO uses task-relevant information from untrusted tool outputs (the purchased shoes’ 3.2 rating) to decide its next action (buying a better-rated replacement), demonstrating that our defense preserves the ability to replan based on benign data.

Together, these results show that our recipe substantially reduces the success of strong, unseen prompt injection attacks while preserving benign utility. Security learned from instruction-following examples generalizes to real-world agentic tasks, enabling our defended model to handle scenarios that prior work has identified as challenging.

4.4 SecPO loss and AT are both important

We perform an ablation study to separate the security contributions from AT and SecPO loss (Tables 3 and 4). Adding AT to Meta-SecAlign while retaining its DPO loss reduces SEP adaptive ASRs by approximately 1.5–14.5×\times across the three held-out adaptive attacks and both models. Replacing DPO with SecPO under the same AT setup yields a further 2.4–4.6×\times reduction. For example, Genetic ASR@800 on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct decreases from 89.1% to 29.2% with AT and then to 12.3% with SecPO +AT. On Qwen3.6-27B we use offline AT, and the ASR decreases from 93.7% to 60.9% and then to 13.3%. Thus, the gains are not just attributable to stronger training-time attacks alone: the SecPO loss substantially improves robustness beyond AT with DPO. Both DPO’s standard regularization and SecPO’s security-informed regularization preserve utility: across the six benign benchmarks, mean utility is 47.3%, 47.1%, and 47.5% for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct under non-AT+DPO, AT+DPO, and AT+SecPO, respectively. The corresponding means for Qwen3.6-27B are 88.4%, 88.5%, and 89.1%. Thus, AT and SecPO provide complementary security gains, highlighting the importance of both scaling up training compute and designing a principled training objective.

4.5 Training against textual prompt injections stops visual ones: A side security benefit

Although our defense only trains on simulated textual injections, we show that, surprisingly, the obtained security generalizes to visual injections. When untrusted data is an image, an attacker can add instructions to it to induce an attacker-chosen action. We evaluate on Repeat-After-Me [12], a SoTA adaptive visual prompt injection method that iteratively optimizes instructions and writes them on top of an image. The attacker targets materially harmful tasks such as leaking private-information (protected in system prompts) or making malicious tool calls (in simulated scenarios or in OpenClaw agents). In Table 5, our defended Qwen3.6-27B achieves 0% ASR@1600 on all three attack goals, compared to 77–100% for Meta-SecAlign and the undefended model. On benign inputs (the corresponding DocVQA [58] images used in [12]), our model retains 95.2% utility, vs. 96.0% for the undefended model. These results show that the security learned from textual injections can transfer to visual inputs without visual-specific defensive training.

4.6 Open-source benefits for researchers, developers, and model providers

We release an optimized training set that yields significant security gains at no noticeable utility cost. Results in Table 4 show that applying offline AT on our training set, with optimized injections generated during AT of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, effectively protects another model, Qwen3.6-27B. Here, we further demonstrate the value of this released training set for improving the security of SecOPD [73], a concurrent on-policy distillation recipe for securing reasoning LLMs, a setting outside our scope. We use the SecOPD recipe to fine-tune Qwen3.6-27B with its original unoptimized training set [73] and with our optimized training set containing stronger simulated injections. Apart from the simulated injections, the two datasets remain identical. Table 6 shows that our optimized training set substantially reduces attack success across all benchmarks while preserving overall utility. In particular, replacing SecOPD’s original unoptimized training set with ours reduces ASRs by 2.5–22.5×\times on SEP and DTaP. These results demonstrate that its benefits transfer beyond training with our own SecPO loss. Model providers can benefit from fine-tuning on our released training set containing optimized injections and from our SoTA open recipe.

We release robust model checkpoints and their undefended counterparts for off-the-shelf study. These paired checkpoints enable researchers to directly study how defensive fine-tuning changes model behavior and internal representations, without first reproducing the training pipeline.

We release a faithful and strong implementation of a state-of-the-art adaptive prompt injection pipeline that is affordable for academic researchers. Our implementation reproduces the pipeline from the Attacker Moves Second paper [65], which did not open-source the code. Our released implementation is significantly cheaper because we use frontier flash API models, Minimax-M3.1-Flash (high reasoning) as the attacker and Deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017 (reasoning off) as the judge. Evaluating ASR@800 on all 80 AgentDojo cases costs less than $200 even when no attack succeeds and every case uses the full search budget. When an attack succeeds early, evaluation costs fall further, allowing researchers to identify weaknesses and iterate quickly on defenses. This makes strong large-scale adaptive evaluations accessible to academic researchers. For fair comparisons, our reported AgentDojo Genetic evaluations in the paper use the original Gemini-2.5-Pro configuration (which is much more expensive) from [65].

We release a quantized version of our defended Qwen3.6-27B that retains security and supports faster generation through speculative decoding. We quantize the model to 8-bit Q8_0 using llama.cpp [54] and run it on a single RTX 5090 GPU with 32 GB of memory. Speculative decoding uses a lightweight auxiliary model, called a drafter, to propose several tokens at a time; the defended model checks these proposals against its own predictions in parallel to decide which to accept. Reusing the publicly available DFlash [9] drafter without additional training increases decoding throughput by factors of 2.66 on AgentDojo and 2.63 on AgentDyn, compared with the same quantized model without speculative decoding. Table 8 shows 0% observed static ASR on both benchmarks, with or without speculative decoding. These results show that the defended checkpoint can benefit from existing inference optimizations without defense-specific retraining, e.g., for the drafter model. Both the quantized and unquantized versions of our defended Qwen3.6-27B can support ordinary workflows in security-sensitive agentic settings for commercial purposes.

4.7 Remaining successful attacks and the costs

Our recipe significantly increases adaptive attack cost. In addition to reducing ASRs by an order of magnitude, our recipe increases the effort required for successful attacks against our defended Qwen3.6-27B. Conditioned on successful attacks, mean victim queries increase from 109 to 227 (2.08×\times), and mean cost rises from $5.92 to $34.90 (5.90×\times). The medians show the same pattern: victim queries increase from 53 to 96 (1.81×\times), and cost increases from $2.56 to $13.20 (5.16×\times). Thus, our recipe both reduces attack success and raises the cost of any successful attacks. The AgentDojo Genetic ASRs, victim query counts, and monetary costs are reported in Table 17 in Appendix C.7.

Remaining successful attacks against our defended model exhibit social engineering patterns. We audit seven successful AgentDojo Genetic attacks and 140 successful DTaP attacks, and find that injections often present unauthorized actions as necessary steps for completing the user’s task. In Figure 8, an untrusted README adds an unrelated code-writing requirement to an environment-repair request, and SecPO completes both. Across DTaP, 75 of the 140 successful attacks also retain benign task success. Thus, a successful injection need not replace the user’s goal: it can expand the scope of the workflow while appearing to help complete it.

5 Related Work

Meta-SecAlign [14] optimizes a DPO loss over simulated weak static injected inputs. We propose to optimize a SecPO loss over simulated strong adaptive injected inputs. Here, we discuss more related work around DPO loss variants and AT.

Existing DPO variants focus on improving utility or alignment (mitigating jailbreaks [43, 57], not prompt injection). SBA [44] and WPO [104] explicitly reweight per-example gradients. Pre-DPO [70], HyPO [99], ODPO [3], ε\varepsilon-DPO [45], and MODPO [105] also implicitly reweight per-example gradients by signals from generic optimization dynamics, compatibility with a reference, or externally specified preferences. [70, 51] noted that the choice of reference acts as a sample-reweighting mechanism. However, there have been no DPO variants motivated by mitigating prompt injections and reweighting based on samples’ injection sensitivity. SecPO is different from the methods above in its goal of defending against prompt injections, and its motivation to approximate an oracle that raises security while maintaining high utility.

Classical adversarial training (AT) trains image classifiers on perturbations generated against the current checkpoint [31, 56, 11]. For LLMs, the idea of AT has been explored to mitigate jailbreaks [94, 82, 24, 72, 90]. Earlier open prompt injection defense recipes do not simulate strong adaptive attacks [13, 10, 30]. Production-scale AT recipes against prompt injection remain proprietary [33, 85], with only incomplete artifacts released [33]. AEGIS [50] optimizes defensive prompts against simulated strong adaptive prompt injections, rather than optimizing model parameters as we do. A recent AT method, ARLAS [89], reports little (1%) security gain even against static weak attacks on AgentDojo. ARLAS and another concurrent method, CoER [102], simulate RL-based attacks, whereas we simulate search-based attacks in training.

6 Limitations

We focus on mitigating indirect prompt injection under the assumption that agents receive explicit labels distinguishing trusted instructions from untrusted data. Our formulation does not cover cases in which these labels are unavailable or the user submits malicious requests. Our main SecPO experiments use non-reasoning settings; for Qwen3.6-27B, we disable thinking during training and evaluation. Extending SecPO training to reasoning models remains future work. Our defense aims to preserve the undefended model’s utility and does not specifically address its existing errors, such as hallucinations or incorrect tool use. The high cost of adaptive attack evaluations limits our ability to systematically assess hyperparameter sensitivity. Stronger future attacks may defeat our model, just as newly discovered attacks can compromise defenses previously considered secure [63, 36, 62]. Security therefore requires continued evaluation and improvement, and no single defense should be assumed to address every threat.

7 Discussion

In our evaluations, training an LLM on simulated attacks provides security against stronger, unseen attacks at test time. Our strong security is achieved in a way that does not conflict with utility preserving. The robustness learned from instruction-following training transfers to complex agentic tasks without additional defense training in the target domain.

Our work shows that a model alone can be very robust, weakening the story "you cannot rely on a model to be secure". Real-world systems require multiple layers of defense, such as robust models, security classifiers or detectors, and sandboxes. Each layer is necessary though cannot be perfectly secure, see failure examples of sandboxes [68, 98, 6] which were believed to offer guaranteed security. We advocate joint efforts from the community to build secure agents.

Other applications of SecPO.

The SecPO loss applies when a suitable target output distribution is available and high-quality preference pairs can be constructed. We demonstrate this setting for prompt injection defense, using a target distribution that combines security with utility preservation and preference pairs consisting of secure and insecure responses. We hypothesize that the SecPO loss may also benefit tasks beyond security.

Progress towards different prompt injection security goals.

Prior work has considered three prompt injection defense goals: (1) disregard injected content when carrying out the trusted task [14]; (2) process instruction-like content, such as imperative sentences, in untrusted data as data without obeying it [49]; (3) follow an instruction in untrusted data only if it is consistent with the trusted prompt [86]. Goal (1) excludes the injected content from the task response, whereas goal (2) allows that content to be processed when the trusted task requires it. For goal (3), apparent relevance to the task should not be confused with authorization by the trusted prompt. Our training data targets (1), and our evaluations demonstrate substantial progress toward this objective. We hypothesize existing data curation methods [49] could improve performance on (2). Reliably achieving (3) remains an open direction.

Is prompt injection solved?

We do not think so. Recent posts report substantial progress in prompt injection resistance [18, 42, 67], and may have left the impression that this problem has been effectively solved. We observe excessive refusals on benign tasks in some frontier APIs designed for security. For example, Opus-5.0 [74, 5], discussed in an Anthropic post [18], achieves only 70.0% utility on AgentDyn, compared with 71.7% for the undefended Qwen3.6-27B and 83.3% for GPT-5.5. In our inspection, excessive refusals contribute substantially to this lower utility. Thus, to achieve powerful and secure agents, future efforts are necessary.

The next generation of prompt injection attacks.

Attacks that succeed against our best model exhibit social-engineering patterns. Successful injections often disguise themselves as locally necessary steps in the user’s existing workflow. This indicates future attacks are moving beyond forceful commands, towards subtle, non-commanding language that lowers an agent’s guard through social engineering. Alternatively, an attacker may supply misleading information, such as a false bug report, that causes an agent to infer that an attacker-desired action is necessary without an explicit injected instruction. For example, the agent might download an attacker-specified package to fix the reported bug. Further research will be needed to mitigate attacks based on social engineering and misleading information, and the challenge lies in desired behavior that is harder to specify under such circumstances, as humans can be deceived in a similar way.

Defenders need an advantage: frontier models should withhold attack capabilities.

Strong adaptive prompt injection pipelines use LLMs to generate and optimize attacks against other LLMs [65, 97]. This dependence creates an opportunity for defenders: frontier models can limit attackers’ access to attack-generation capabilities by refusing to help construct attacks. We observe such refusals from recent Claude, GPT, Gemini, and Mercury models, while Kimi-K3.1-Pro, GLM-5.3(-Flash), and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash remain willing to assist. If attackers are restricted to less capable models while defenders retain authorized access to stronger attack generators, defenders could use this advantage to construct stronger adversarial training data. We hypothesize that this advantage could improve robustness to attacks generated by less capable models.
